title: Local Elections Are Telling Us Something
standfirst: Small swings in council seats point to a larger shift.
body: Local elections rarely make the front pages for long. Turnout is low, the issues are bins and potholes, and national commentators treat the results as a rough opinion poll. That is a mistake. Read carefully, they often show change before it reaches Westminster.

The most telling results are not the big council takeovers but the steady drip of by-elections. A seat here, a seat there, won by a party that held nothing in the area a few years ago. Each one is small. Together they trace a pattern.

Independents and residents’ groups have also done well in many places. Voters who are tired of national parties often trust a local name they recognise, someone who answers their emails and turns up to the parish meeting.
## Why it matters for the country

Councillors are the foot soldiers of national parties. They knock on doors, deliver leaflets and know their wards street by street. A party that loses its councillors loses its ground game, and that weakness shows up at the next general election.

Low turnout means local results can exaggerate swings, and protest votes do not always carry over to a general election. The trick is to look for consistency. One surprising result is noise. The same surprise in town after town is a signal worth taking seriously.
